newsitem.title: USA: IMF delays $40 million Croatia loan.
newsitem.headline: IMF delays $40 million Croatia loan.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund decided on Friday to postpone the release of a $40 million credit to Croatia in a bid to convince Zagreb to live up to the terms of the Dayton peace pact, U.S. officials said.
"We have begun to see some more serious efforts by Croatia," Robert Gelbard, President Clinton's special representative for the region, told Reuters. "They need to do much, much more."
The decision by the IMF board came despite growing uneasiness among some European and other nations that such a move could lead to the politicization of the Fund.

The $40 million is the second tranche of a $486 million, three-year IMF loan for Croatia approved by the IMF earlier this year. Zagreb has fulfilled all the economic conditions set out under the loan agreement.
In a statement released in Zagreb, the Croatian central bank said the IMF decision would not seriously affect the country's finances.

"The denial of the expected credit tranche will not have a direct significant impact on financial conditions of Croatia," the central bank said, noting the country has $4.7 billion in foreign currency reserves.

Although the bank said the IMF had postponed release of the tranche indefinitely, monetary sources here said the board agreed to take up the issue again in the fall, possibly on Sept. 10, but no later than Oct. 10.

U.S. officials listed a number of areas where they believe that Croatia is not living up to the terms of the 1995 Dayton peace agreement, including turning in war criminals and allowing freedom of movement for refugees.
A senior Treasury official, who declined to be named, said there was broad support on the IMF board for the decision to delay consideration of the release of the loan.

However, some monetary sources, who also requested anonymity, voiced concern at the move. While agreeing with the goal of getting Croatia to comply with Dayton peace accord, they questioned whether this was the best way to do that.

"Several European countries are very concerned that this decision will politicize the Fund too much" by putting political conditions on an economic loan program that has already been agreed to, one source said.

U.S. officials though argued that Croatia would be unable to repay the loan and carry through with the economic reforms required under the credit if hostilities broke out in the region. That justifies holding up release of the credit until Zagreb lives up the Dayton peace pact, they said.
The IMF's decision to postpone consideration of the Croatia loan is the latest in a series of steps aimed at putting pressure on Zagreb to comply with the peace agreement.
Both the World Bank and the European Bank for Reconstruction and Development have recently delayed consideration of new loans for Croatia.
